lesson.grammar_point: quantifiers with countable and uncountable nouns

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: f
the money a university charges you to study there
c
the goods that a ship, a truck or a plane is carrying
a
how much there is of something you cannot count one by one, like money or sugar
i
facts about something — one word that never takes an s and never takes an a
g
one unit of study that counts toward a degree
j
one of the things you are allowed to choose
d
how much space or how much material there is, once somebody measures it
e
the maximum a country or a company allows in a period
b
how many there are of something you can count, like ships or clauses
h
something in a contract that has to be true, or the deal does not hold

paras: Bianca Feltrin works in operations at a trading house in Santos, and her job is a list of numbers. A vessel is coming from Rotterdam. It is going to load sixty thousand tons of sugar, and the buyer has eleven days to do it. If the loading takes twelve days, somebody pays for the extra day, and the amount is already written in the contract, months before anybody sees the ship.

She says people outside the market imagine a lot of drama and very little arithmetic. It is the opposite. There is not much drama. There are a few difficult calls a month, and almost all of them are about a quantity that does not match: the volume on the shipping documents, the volume the buyer expected, or a quota that changed in the middle of the shipment.

The words matter as much as the figures. "We need some information about the cargo" is a normal sentence in her week. "We need an information" is not, and the other side notices. A ship can be late by a few hours or by a little time; it cannot be late by a few time. Bianca learned that in her first year, in an email that went to four countries at once.

Her son is applying to a master's degree abroad this year, and she says the paperwork is the same job with other nouns. How many credits does the program have? How much tuition does it cost, and how many payments? Are there any conditions for the second year, and how many options does he have if the answer is no? Every question is a quantity, and every wrong answer costs money later. She reads his forms the way she reads a contract: line by line, looking for the number that does not fit.
reading.source: A composite portrait of a Santos trading desk, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain how sugar is produced and exported from Brazil.
To show that the work is counting — and that the words around the numbers cost as much as the numbers.
To argue that operations is a more difficult job than law.

items.situation: Ask me two questions about the cargo: one with how much, one with how many.
tips: How much sugar is on that vessel? How many days do we have to load it?
Sugar is measured, days are counted. That is the whole rule.

items.situation: Say the same idea twice: once about time, once about calls.
tips: We have a little time. We have a few calls.
A little goes with what you measure, a few with what you count.

items.situation: Correct me. I say: 'I need an information about the quota.'
tips: I need some information about the quota.
Information never takes an a and never takes an s. Same for tuition and cargo.

items.situation: Say what your firm does NOT have much of, and what it has a lot of.
tips: We do not have much time in December, and we have a lot of contracts.
Not much for the measured one, a lot of for both.

items.situation: Ask me three questions about a master's program, all about quantity.
tips: How many credits does it have? How much does the tuition cost? Are there any conditions for the second year?

items.situation: One shipment of yours, in numbers. Tell me four of them.
tips: Forty thousand tons, three ports, eleven days, and one quota that changes in July.

listenings.text: Good morning, this is the operations note for the sugar vessel. Four numbers, and then I am done. First: sixty thousand tons, and the buyer has eleven days to load them. Second: we already have some information from the terminal, but not much, and I am waiting for the rest this afternoon. Third: the export quota changed on Friday, so please do not use the figure from the old table. There are a few contracts in the folder with the old number, and I am correcting them today. Fourth, and this is the one that costs money: if the loading takes more than eleven days, the extra time has a price, and that price is already in the contract. Nobody negotiates it when the problem happens. We only pay it.

Every year I meet people who choose a program by the ranking and then discover the arithmetic in September. So let me give you the four questions to ask before you sign anything. How many credits does the degree have, and how many of them are compulsory? How much is the tuition, and how many payments can you make? Are there any conditions attached to the second year, like a minimum grade or a language certificate? And finally: if you cannot start in September, how many options do you actually have? Notice that not one of those questions is about the ranking. A little information at the right moment is worth a lot of regret later, and most of that information is on a page that almost nobody opens.
